additions.title: OECD AI Principles: Transparency and explainability (Principle 1.3)
additions.quote: to make stakeholders aware of their interactions with AI systems, including in the workplace
additions.why: International comparator. The intergovernmental principle asks AI actors to make people aware they are dealing with AI, and extends it to the workplace, which the UK consumer-law route does not. The OECD's own page for the principle; the legal instrument itself (OECD/LEGAL/0449) could not be read because its site needs JavaScript, and the page shows no adoption or revision date. A non-binding recommendation to governments, not a rule for firms. Year is that of first adoption, from background knowledge.

additions.title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
additions.locator: Paragraph 127 (policy area on communication and information / human-AI interaction); see also paragraph 38, last sentence
additions.quote: users can easily identify whether they are interacting with a living being, or with an AI system imitating human or animal characteristics
additions.why: The global standard adopted by UNESCO's General Conference. Paragraph 127 adds a right to refuse the interaction and ask for a person; paragraph 38 says users should be told when a service is provided with AI. Addressed to states, non-binding, and written before generative chatbots were common.

additions.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
additions.publisher: Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission, Singapore
additions.quote: an online portal may inform its users that they are interacting with an AI-powered chatbot and not a human customer service agent
additions.why: Comparator from Singapore: a regulator-issued, voluntary framework that treats disclosure of a chatbot as the basic example of general disclosure. Voluntary ('encouraged'), dated 2020 and not updated for generative AI in this edition.

additions.title: California Business and Professions Code, section 17941 (Bots)
additions.locator: s.17941(a) and (b); added by Stats. 2018, Ch. 892 (SB 1001), operative 1 July 2019
additions.quote: A person using a bot shall not be liable under this section if the person discloses that it is a bot.
additions.why: The earliest statute found that makes disclosure the safe harbour. Narrower than it is often described: it bites only where a bot is used with intent to mislead in order to sell goods or services or influence a vote. Disclosure must be 'clear, conspicuous, and reasonably designed'. US state law, no effect in the UK.

additions.title: California Senate Bill No. 243 (Companion chatbots), Chapter 677, Statutes of 2025
additions.locator: Section 1, adding Business and Professions Code s.22602(a)
additions.quote: an operator shall issue a clear and conspicuous notification indicating that the companion chatbot is artificially generated and not human
additions.why: A 2025 statute that uses a reasonable-person test close to the EU's 'obvious' exception: notification is owed where a reasonable person would be misled into thinking they are talking to a human. Covers companion chatbots only. Chaptered bill text; the operative date and any later amendment were not checked. US state law.

additions.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
additions.locator: Principle 7: You are open and collaborative
additions.quote: You should also clearly identify any automated response to the public.
additions.why: The UK government's own standard for public bodies, with example wording for a chatbot reply ('this response has been written by an automated AI chatbot'). Guidance for the public sector, not a duty on companies; useful as a benchmark for what 'exceeds the legal floor' looks like in the UK.

additions.title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, section 226: Misleading actions
additions.quote: an overall presentation which is likely to deceive the average consumer about a matter relating to a product, a trader or any other matter
additions.why: The second consumer-law route alongside misleading omissions: an agent presented so that people take it for a person can deceive by overall presentation even if nothing false is said. The section does not mention AI; applying it to chatbots is a reading of the CMA's guidance, not a court ruling.

additions.title: Frontiers: Machines vs. Humans: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Disclosure on Customer Purchases
additions.publisher: Luo, Tong, Fang and Qu, Marketing Science 38(6)
additions.quote: reduces purchase rates by more than 79.7%
additions.why: Peer-reviewed field experiment on more than 6,200 customers: disclosing the chatbot before an outbound sales call cut purchases sharply. Shows the commercial incentive not to disclose, which is why a written standard is needed. A single firm's structured outbound sales calls, with 2019 technology; the copy read is hosted by the lead author's university (Temple), and the journal's own site was not read.

additions.title: Trust me, I'm a bot: repercussions of chatbot disclosure in different service frontline settings
additions.publisher: Mozafari, Weiger and Hammerschmidt, Journal of Service Management
additions.quote: Chatbot disclosure has a negative indirect effect on customer retention through mitigated trust for services with high criticality.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed. Two scenario experiments: disclosure costs trust where the service matters a great deal, but helps retention when the chatbot fails to solve the problem. Supports user-testing the wording and placement instead of assuming disclosure is neutral. Simulated interactions, not live customers; copy hosted by the authors' university (Goettingen).

additions.title: Large Language Models Pass the Turing Test
additions.quote: GPT-4.5 was judged to be the human 73% of the time
additions.why: Why silence now deceives: in pre-registered three-party tests, people picked a prompted language model as the human more often than the real person. Weakens any reliance on the interaction being 'obvious'. Preprint, not peer reviewed on the date checked; five-minute text chats in two participant pools.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. One reading-list note is dated: the Commission's Article 50 page no longer carries a 'not yet updated' notice; it now says the text is the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with only paragraph 7 marked AMENDED. The guidelines landing page says the Commission 'adopted' the guidelines; whether formal adoption has now happened was not confirmed.
